newsitem.title: SPAIN: SUPREME COURT EXAMINES "DIRTY WAR" PAPERS.
newsitem.headline: SUPREME COURT EXAMINES "DIRTY WAR" PAPERS.

text.p: Spain's Supreme Court examined on Wednesday secret files purporting to prove the former Socialist government set up death squads which waged a "dirty war" against ETA Basque separatists.

In an unprecedented move, the court's 33 judges studied 18 spy documents on microfilm under high security for five hours to decide firstly if they are legitimate and then if they should be declassified for possible use as evidence in court.
The session ended with no announcement of a decision and no date was set for a ruling.

Lower courts investigating a secret campaign of bombings, kidnap, torture and murder against ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) say the documents of military intelligence agency CESID contain vital information needed to try high-ranking officials and former security chiefs.

Alleged copies leaked to the press suggest the former Socialist government of Felipe Gonzalez was responsible for organising the death squads known as Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups (GAL) which killed 28 people in the 1980s.
Both the ruling conservative Popular Party (PP) government and its Socialist predecessor have said the files should remain secret for state security reasons.
But the Supreme Court asked last week to examine them and Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar authorised the temporary, high security transfer of the files.

Spain's secret service head, Lt-General Javier Calderon, personally delivered the papers to the court accompanied by a police escort. Local media said it was the first time the judges had had access to information classified as state secrets.
The Supreme Court judges began to scan the "dirty war" files just 48 hours after ETA attackers claimed the life of one of their colleagues, Rafael Martinez.

He was fatally shot in the head outside his house in central Madrid, in what the High Court interpreted as a reprisal for the imprisonment of several leaders of ETA's political wing, Herri Batasuna (HB).
ETA struck back hard this week, killing a military base hairdresser with a car bomb in southern Spain on Monday and shooting dead a businessman in the Basque region on Tuesday.
The government has vowed to pursue its hard line against the guerrillas and says it will not be forced to the negotiating table.

Families of alleged ETA victims killed by GAL are determined to take the former Socialist government to task for the "dirty war". Senior officials, including former interior minister Jose Barrionuevo, have been charged in the case.
Allegations that the Socialists were responsible for setting up death squads contribued to the election defeat of Gonzalez last March after 13 years in power.
